claim: Digits to Dollars estimates Apple's total merchant-silicon-equivalent cost (if Apple bought chips instead of designing its own) at roughly $10 billion per year, based on iPhone/iPad processor costs of $30-40 and Mac CPU costs of ~$100, applied to ~200M iPhones, 18M Macs, and 30M iPads -- about 10% of Apple's ~$130 billion hardware COGS at the time.
stance_target: Owning silicon is load-bearing for margin (baseline sizing)
scope_conditions: FY2020 estimate, author's own rough model, cross-checked against a Nikkei iPhone 12 teardown ($406 total BOM, ~$40 A14 chip, also ~10%)
quoted_support: Multiply all that out and we get about $10 billion in silicon cost. Apple's cost of goods sold for hardware last year totaled about $130 billion, so silicon is a little bit less than 10% of that.

claim: Digits to Dollars' own-silicon manufacturing cost model, based on die-per-wafer geometry (iPhone/iPad chips ~90-100mm2, M1 ~120mm2 yielding 500-666 die per wafer) and an assumed $15,000/wafer TSMC price, estimates total wafer cost at ~$6.4 billion -- implying a raw saving of ~$3.5 billion versus the ~$10 billion merchant-silicon equivalent, worth about 1.7 percentage points of hardware gross margin.
stance_target: Owning silicon is load-bearing for margin
scope_conditions: FY2020 estimate, author's own rough model; explicitly caveated as possibly 'wildly off'
quoted_support: TSMC probably charges something like $15,000/wafer yielding a total cost of $6.4 billion. So Apple is saving $3.5 billion or so versus using merchant silicon. This alone is worth 1.7% pts of gross margin.

claim: Once the design team is priced in (estimated at ~5,000 engineers, ~$2 billion/year) plus ASIC/backend, test, assembly and packaging fees (assumed largely paid to Broadcom), total fully-loaded in-house silicon cost rises to approximately $9 billion, nearly matching the ~$10 billion it would cost Apple to simply buy merchant silicon -- the central contrarian finding.
stance_target: Owning silicon is load-bearing for margin
scope_conditions: FY2020 estimate, author's own rough model; design team headcount is an assumption, not disclosed by Apple
quoted_support: Then factor in fees they pay to ASIC vendors, probably Broadcom ... and we get to $9 billion in total cost for Apple Silicon. Compare that to the $10 billion or so it would cost to buy merchant silicon and something becomes clear -- Apple is not saving that much money by building its own silicon.

claim: The full contrarian thesis, stated explicitly: fully loaded for R&D and design-team cost, Apple Silicon may even be MORE expensive than buying merchant silicon -- directly negating the query's premise that silicon ownership is a durable margin advantage via COGS reduction.
stance_target: Owning silicon is load-bearing for margin
scope_conditions: Author's own model, self-described as rough and possibly understating design costs
quoted_support: We could make the argument that factoring in all costs and even larger design teams than we modeled here, that Apple Silicon may even be more expensive than using merchant silicon. ... Apple is not into silicon for the money.

claim: The real benefit of Apple Silicon is strategic/experiential differentiation that drives ASP and unit sales, not COGS reduction: faster, more responsive, less power-hungry products sell more units at premium prices, which the author values above direct cost savings.
stance_target: Silicon's contribution shows up in COGS/margin rather than in ASP/pricing power
scope_conditions: Author's interpretive argument, not a quantified model
quoted_support: Saving $75 on a $2000 laptop is nice, but selling one more $2,000 laptop because of the silicon is much better.

claim: Custom silicon functions as a competitive barrier to entry in smartphones: companies without their own chip design are being marginalized to low-price, low-profit segments, and losing chip access (as with Huawei, cut off from advanced chip supply) can eliminate a company from the premium smartphone business entirely.
stance_target: Durability of silicon-based competitive moat (differentiation framing)
quoted_support: To compete in phones, companies need their own silicon or risk being marginalized to low price, low profit segments ... this shows why Huawei is no longer in the phone business, now that they cannot build their own chips.

claim: Rival Android OEMs (Oppo/Vivo, Xiaomi) were independently investing heavily in their own custom processor design as of 2020, indicating the industry consensus was converging on Apple's vertical-integration strategy rather than the gap being uniquely defensible.
stance_target: Whether merchant-silicon competitors are closing the gap
quoted_support: Oppo/Vivo and Xiaomi are investing heavily in designing their own processors.
